title: A Great Light and a Child Is Born
summary: The gloom that closed chapter 8 gives way to light: the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, humbled in the past, will be honored, and the people walking in darkness see a great light. The oppressor's yoke is broken because a child is born, a son given, who will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, and will reign on David's throne forever. Then the chapter turns to the northern kingdom's pride and describes three waves of judgment, each ending with the refrain that God's anger is not turned away.
story: Chapter 8 ended with the people driven into darkness after rejecting God's word in the Assyrian crisis. Chapter 9 answers that darkness with the most famous royal promise in Isaiah. Ahaz, the king of chapter 7, had failed the test of faith; here God promises a king from David's line who will be everything Ahaz was not. The Immanuel sign of 7:14 grows into this portrait of a child with divine titles. The second half of the chapter (verses 8-21) returns to the present and begins a poem against Israel, the northern kingdom, whose refrain first appeared in 5:25 and continues into 10:4. Promise and judgment stand side by side, as they do throughout Isaiah's opening chapters.
historical:
Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal territories in Galilee, the northern part of Israel. The way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, and Galilee of the nations (verse 1) correspond closely to the regions Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria annexed in 733 to 732 BC, which he organized as Assyrian provinces. Second Kings 15:29 lists Galilee and all the land of Naphtali among the areas he took and deported. These were the first parts of Israel to fall into darkness, and Isaiah promises they will be the first to see light.

The day of Midian (verse 4) recalls Gideon's victory over the Midianites with a small band, when God, not military strength, won the battle (Judges 7). Verses 8 to 21 address the northern kingdom in the years before its fall in 722 BC. Its people responded to early losses with defiant confidence (verse 10), and its politics were violent: four of its last six kings were assassinated (2 Kings 15). Aram and Philistia (verse 12) had both taken territory from Israel. Verse 21's picture of Manasseh and Ephraim devouring each other matches the civil strife of those last decades.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East a king's accession was accompanied by throne names and titles. Egyptian pharaohs, for example, received a set of formal names at their coronation, and some scholars have suggested that the four names of verse 6 reflect a similar practice, perhaps as names announced at a royal birth or enthronement. The titles go far beyond anything claimed for a Judean king, however. Mighty God (El Gibbor) is used of the Lord himself in 10:21, and Everlasting Father describes a king who cares for his people like a father forever.

A yoke was the wooden bar laid across the neck of an ox or of captives, and the rod or bar across the shoulders was a symbol of forced labor. Burning boots and blood-soaked garments (verse 5) pictures the end of war: the gear of soldiers is gathered and burned because it will never be needed again. Palm branch and reed (verse 14) are an image of high and low, the whole social order. Bricks and sycamores (verse 10) were the ordinary building materials; dressed stone and cedar were the materials of palaces. Israel's response to disaster was to promise grander rebuilding rather than repentance.
literary: The chapter has two very different parts. Verses 1 to 7 are a royal hymn of salvation, moving from darkness to light, from oppression to joy, and from war to peace, with three reasons each introduced by for (verses 4, 5, and 6). The birth of the child is the climax and the ground of all the rest. Verses 8 to 21 are a judgment poem in three stanzas (verses 8-12, 13-17, 18-21), each ending with the refrain “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” A fourth stanza follows in 10:1-4, and the same refrain appears in 5:25, which suggests that these poems were once connected. The contrast is deliberate: Israel's human kings and leaders lead to ruin, while the promised king brings peace without end.

outline.t: Light for the lands in darkness
Joy, the broken yoke, and the end of war
Unto us a child is born
Israel's pride and the first judgment
Leaders cut off, head and tail

doctrines.note: The child of verses 6 and 7 is the clearest picture so far of the coming king: born into David's line, bearing divine titles, reigning with justice and righteousness forever. Christians confess this child as Jesus.
The promised kingdom grows without end and rests on justice and righteousness, not conquest. It is established by the zeal of the Lord, not human effort.
The poem of verses 8 to 21 shows judgment answering persistent refusal to repent. Each blow is meant to turn the people back, and each time they refuse, the anger continues.
Hope begins where the darkness was deepest, in the lands first conquered. The pattern of darkness to light shapes the Bible's whole account of salvation.

words.note: El, God, in the title El Gibbor, Mighty God, in verse 6. Some interpreters render the phrase as godlike hero or mighty warrior, as a royal title. But the identical phrase in 10:21 clearly refers to the Lord, which makes Mighty God the natural reading and marks this child as more than an ordinary king.

Pele, wonder, part of the title Wonderful Counselor. The word is used of God's extraordinary acts, such as the wonders of the exodus (Exodus 15:11). The child's counsel will be of a kind that only God gives, in contrast to Ahaz's disastrous political counsel.

Shalom, peace, appearing twice: in the title Prince of Peace and in the endless increase of peace (verses 6-7). Shalom means more than the absence of war; it is wholeness, security, and right relationship in every direction.

Or, light. In verse 2 it is the great light that dawns on people living in darkness and the shadow of death. Light in Isaiah stands for God's saving presence, and the same image returns in 60:1-3, where the glory of the Lord rises on Zion.

christ: Matthew 4:12-17 quotes verses 1 and 2 when Jesus begins his ministry in Capernaum, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, and sees in it the fulfillment of the great light dawning in Galilee. The child of verses 6 and 7 is read throughout Christian history as Jesus. The angel's announcement to Mary that her son will be given the throne of David and that his kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32-33) echoes verse 7 closely. The titles Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace describe the one Christians confess as fully God and fully human, the Son who was given. Christians have long sung these words at Christmas, most famously in Handel's Messiah. Ephesians 2:14 calls Christ our peace, and Colossians 1:13 speaks of being rescued from the domain of darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.

hard.q: Were the titles in verse 6 meant for a human king of Isaiah's day, or for a divine Messiah?
hard.a: Interpreters differ. Many Jewish readers, ancient and modern, have identified the child with Hezekiah, Ahaz's son, whose faith and reforms stood in contrast to his father, and some Jewish translations render the four titles as a single sentence-name that speaks about God, so that the name declares what God plans rather than describing the child himself. Some critical scholars also read the verse as a coronation hymn for a Judean king, perhaps Hezekiah or Josiah, in the extravagant style of royal courts. Christian interpreters generally read it as a messianic prophecy fulfilled in Jesus, noting that the title Mighty God is used of the Lord himself in 10:21, that the kingdom has no end, and that no historical king of Judah fulfilled the promise of endless peace. Some Christians combine the two, seeing a royal hope that no son of David in Isaiah's time could fulfill and that the New Testament finds realized in Jesus. The text itself pushes beyond any ordinary king in its language of an eternal reign.

questions: The light dawns first on the lands that suffered first. Where have you seen hope arrive in the darkest places?
Which of the four names in verse 6 speaks most directly to what you need from God right now, and why?
Israel responded to disaster by promising to rebuild bigger (verse 10) rather than returning to God. How do people repeat that pattern today?
